newsitem.title: CANADA: British Columbia sees C$185 mln deficit in 97/98.
newsitem.headline: British Columbia sees C$185 mln deficit in 97/98.

text.p: The Canadian province of British Columbia on Tuesday forecast a budget deficit of C$185 million for the 1997/98 fiscal year ended March 31, down from a C$395 million deficit in 1996/97.

The government also reported a C$772 million deficit for the first 10 months of 1996/97, but said this figure would fall to C$395 million at year-end due to a cyclical late surge in revenues. It said direct provincial government debt would climb by C$837 million in 1996/97.
British Columbia's original 1996/97 budget tabled a year ago projected a surplus of C$87 million.

Under threat of a credit-rating downgrade, the New Democratic Party (NDP) government is expected to face tough questions about its latest budget. Opposition legislators have accused Premier Glen Clark and other officials of lying to voters about the province's finances.

The NDP was re-elected last May after promising a balanced budget for 1995/96 and a budget surplus for this year. But weeks after winning the election, the government admitted its revenue projections were overly optimistic and the budget was actually in deficit for 1995/96.
The government later revealed that the province would not deliver on its promise of a surplus for 1996/97 and initially estimated the year's deficit at C$235 million.

Finance Minister Andrew Petter said the economic climate was tough and he told critics to judge the government by its performance at the end of 1997/98. "...You will see we mean what we say," he told reporters. "It's important we demonstrate we have a commitment to achieve these targets."
But he noted that weaker than expected growth meant that "government revenues are below projections for the fiscal year just ending and...will remain low in the coming fiscal year."
Despite the gloom, the province promised a balanced budget in 1998/99 and projected a surplus of C$110 million for 1999/2000. Future surpluses will be used to pay off direct government debt.

For 1997/98, it said government revenues would rise 0.4 percent to C$20.3 billion. Spending will fall for the first time since 1958, dropping 0.5 percent to C$20.5 billion. The province will proceed with a two percent income tax cut on top of a two percent cut last year and is maintaining tax breaks for small business and a freeze on car insurance premiums, university tuitions and electricity rates.

Petter said the forecasts were based on a "prudent" assumption of 1.6 percent growth in gross domestic product (GDP), even though the government believes the economy will grow 2.2 percent in 1997 and 2.5 percent in 1998.

The government plans C$1.1 billion in capital spending annually over the next three years for schools, hospitals, roads and other infrastructure. It estimated capital spending needs are actually C$1.7 billion a year for the next five years, but said it would "constrain" expenditures by C$600 million annually for the coming three years.

British Columbia's total net borrowing will rise by C$1.4 billion in 1997/98 compared to a C$648 million increase in 1996/97. The province's direct debt, excluding borrowing by crown corporations and other guaranteed debt, will increase C$530 million in 1997/98 to C$11.6 billion.
Total debt will reach C$30.9 billion next March from a current level of C$29.4 billion, but the province said its debt servicing costs remained among the lowest of any Canadian province.

The government said it planned to increase its floating-rate debt exposure over the course of the coming fiscal year. As a proportion of total government direct and financing authority debt, floating-rate borrowing will rise to between 35 percent and 40 percent from the current 24 percent.

The government confirmed it would not meet debt-management targets set in a 1995 plan. Under that plan, direct government debt, which now totals C$11.1 billion, was to have fallen to C$9.6 billion at the end of 1996/97 and to C$9.5 billion at the end of 1997/98.
Petter said the original targets were overly ambitious and exceeded the benchmarks recommended by outside experts.

On the revenue side, the government said it expected higher revenues from several sources including C$170 million in asset sales, a C$89 million dividend increase from the provincially owned electricity utility, C$57 million more from gambling revenues and C$99 million in dividends from other Crown corporations including some from the sale of assets.

The province also expects a 14.7 percent increase in user fees, proceeds from sales of Crown land, license rates and revenues from photo-radar ticketing of speeding vehicles. It also seeks stiffer tobacco tax enforcement.

The financial contribution to the province from Canada's federal government will drop 9 percent or C$200 million from the prior year. Provincial corporate income taxes are expected to be down by C$300 million.
